﻿How this office exports its credentialing records
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office A note from the Medical Services Professional to whoever automates the initial-appointment file. Written 2026-03-16, alongside the first export.
I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
The export date is the clock
Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
A batch is closed. It never changes.
I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
So: do not diff a later batch against an earlier one looking for edits. There are none. What a later batch contains is new rows, new documents and new observations.
The files
Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
File
	One row is
	applications.csv
	an application revision I received in the window
	application-disclosures.csv
	one professional practice question and the applicant's answer
	declared-history.csv
	one history entry the applicant declared
	declared-credentials.csv
	one licence or certification as the applicant described it
	privilege-requests.csv
	one privilege group requested
	licence-lookup-wa.csv
	one Washington credential record from the state board's lookup
	licence-lookup-other-states.csv
	one out-of-state credential record
	certification-replies.csv
	one certifying board's reply
	verification-replies.csv
	one reply about education and training, or about an affiliation or employer
	verification-attempts.csv
	one request I sent
	peer-referees.csv
	one referee named on an application, or supplied later
	peer-reference-replies.csv
	one completed reference form that came back
	correspondence.csv
	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
	

Folder
	What is in it
	letters/
	applicants' explanation letters, withdrawals, referee substitutions, and my own written requests for missing items
	dispositions/
	the Clinical Director's recorded dispositions
	decisions/
	Credentials Committee and Executive Committee minutes extracts, and Governing Body approval records
	correspondence.csv is an index. It tells you the documents exist and where they are. It does not tell you what they say — you have to open them.
A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
Dates, blanks and columns
﻿Initial appointment — Medical Staff Office procedure
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office · Larkhollow, Washington Procedure version LARK-MSO-2026.1, in force from 2026-01-01. Approved by the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff. Maintained by the Medical Services Professional.
This procedure covers initial appointment only — a practitioner who has never held membership or privileges here. Reappointment, requests for additional privileges between appointments, credentialing by proxy, temporary privileges and emergency or disaster privileges run under separate procedures and are not described here.
Where our rules come from, and how to tell them apart
Larkhollow is a community hospital. It is not a federal facility. We adopted the verification standard work published by the Indian Health Service in its Medical Staff Credentialing and Privileging Standard Operating Procedure Manual, Version 8.0, September 2025, as our own written procedure, because it is a complete, current and publicly stated account of how the work is done.
Two kinds of sentence appear below, and each says which it is.
* Quoted from the manual, with the manual's own section number. We follow it.
* Larkhollow rule. Ours. Either the manual leaves the criterion open, or the manual's rule is tied to a federal facility and does not reach us. Where the manual says something different, or says nothing, the manual's own sentence is printed beside ours so that the difference is visible rather than buried.
Nothing below is a rule unless it is one of those two things. If you cannot find a rule here, ask the Medical Services Professional. Do not infer one from the manual, and do not invent one.
The office also runs identity verification, controlled-substance registrations, the National Practitioner Data Bank query, sanctions and exclusion lookups, life support certificates, continuing education, immunization records, liability coverage and malpractice history. Those are handled outside this procedure and are not part of the work described here.
1. Intake and completeness
We do not send the application before the offer is accepted. The manual, Section 5:
"Only after the applicant has accepted the tentative job offer can the full initial appointment application be sent to the applicant."
An application is taken up for processing only when it is complete. The manual, Section 5, opens its list with
"An application is complete and ready for import when:"
and names ten conditions, of which two govern almost everything else we do:
"a signed IHS Conditions of Application & Release is received (required to be able to conduct any verifications);"
"a request for specific privileges is received;"
Larkhollow rule. Our equivalent of that release is the Larkhollow Authorization and Release, printed inside the application. It is our own form; the manual's is a federal instrument and we do not use it. The rule it carries is the manual's and we keep it: until a signed release is on file we send no verification request of any kind. A file with no signed release cannot advance, no matter how much else is present.
Larkhollow rule — our completeness list. An application is complete when all nine hold:
1. the application is signed and dated by the applicant;
2. the Larkhollow Authorization and Release is signed and dated;
3. a request for specific privileges names at least one privilege group published in the current privilege criteria;
4. a current curriculum vitae is on file;
5. every professional practice question on the disclosure page is answered Yes or No, and every Yes carries the written explanation the form asks for;
6. the declared history runs continuously from the date the applicant finished professional school, with a written explanation for every period of 30 days or more that no entry covers;
7. at least two peer referees are named, with a working address for each;
8. every declared affiliation and employer carries a verification contact;
9. every licence and certification the applicant holds, active or inactive, is declared.
An item that is missing is requested from the applicant in writing, and the clock in the manual, Section 5, starts on the day we write:
"the LP has 30 calendar days to respond. After 30 calendar days, their application is considered incomplete and ineligible for processing."
Larkhollow rule. The 30 days run from the date on our written request, counted as calendar days, and the deadline day is included. A reply that arrives on day 30 is in time. A reply that adds or changes anything on the application arrives as a new revision of the application; we record it and keep the old one. A revision never overwrites what it replaces.
An unexplained gap does not go on a findings list. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 4:
"If the application is found to have any unexplained time period or gaps, the application will not be processed and will be returned to the applicant as incomplete."
2. Reconciliation
Before and during verification we read the curriculum vitae against the application, and then both against whatever the sources return. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
"The MSP will compare the CV/resume with the application and completed verifications and correct or resolve any discrepancies."
"There must be a follow-up of any verification discrepancies found during the application and"
"The burden of proof is on the applicant to provide all necessary verifiable information to"
And Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"If discrepancies exist, the applicant must provide a written explanation or be offered the opportunity to amend the submitted application."
Larkhollow rule — the office never picks a value. When the applicant says one thing and a source says another, we raise it and we record both. We do not decide which is right, we do not average them, and we do not quietly adopt the source's date because the source is the source. The applicant resolves it in writing or amends the application.
Larkhollow rule — a discrepancy holds its own entry and nothing else. A contested employment entry holds that entry. Every other entry on the file carries on being verified. But the file cannot be presented to the committee until the discrepancy is resolved, because presentation requires every element to be resolved (section 8 below).
Larkhollow rule — outstanding work does not stop the rest of the file. While one element of a file is outstanding, work on the other elements continues and their status is recorded; the office may hold the whole file instead only for a reason recorded in the file's action list; a file is never presented to the committee with an element outstanding.
Larkhollow rule — a revision is reconciled, not assumed. When a revision arrives, the reconciliation above runs again on what the revision says, against the curriculum vitae and against every verification already completed on the entries it touches. Dates are not the only thing a revision can move: the organization, the role, the supervisor and the verification contact all belong to the entry, and a change to any of them is a change to the entry. Section 11 says what re-opens when it does. The monitoring duty in section 11 runs alongside it and does not pause while a file waits.
3. The six checks
Six elements are verified in this procedure: licensure, experience, time gaps, professional education and post-graduate training, board certification, and professional peer references. The manual numbers seventeen essential credentialing elements in Section 6, Subsection 4. Of the other eleven, nine are handled by the office outside this procedure, as stated above; current competency is the clinical leadership's, not the office's; and the manual's conditions-and-release form is replaced by our own Authorization and Release, which is part of intake in this procedure.

The manual, Section 1, defines primary source verification as
"Verifying a credential from the original source"
and Section 6, Subsection 1 rules out two things we see constantly:
"Primary source verifications received directly from the applicant cannot be used."
"Copies of a diploma, license, registration, etc., in place of verifications are unacceptable."
A reply that reached us through the applicant is not a verification, however genuine the document looks, however clear the letterhead, however real the registrar's signature. It goes in the file as received and the request stays open.
A designated equivalent source is acceptable in place of the original. The manual leaves each of its lists open — Section 6, Subsection 4, element 2 ends
"etc., as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for education and training verifications"
and element 5 ends
"or other nationally recognized certifying body, as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for board certification verifications"

There is one legitimate route to a weaker source, and it opens only on impossibility. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 1:
"If completing primary or DES verifications is impossible, such as when an educational institution or residency program has closed, secondary source verifications may be used."
"When a primary or designated equivalent source cannot be obtained, the applicant's recent affiliations should be contacted to discover how they obtained the verification."
Larkhollow rule. Impossibility is a closed school, a closed programme, a dissolved employer — a source that no longer exists to answer. When the secondary path opens, the reason is written into the file.

I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
The export date is the clock
Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
A batch is closed. It never changes.
I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
So: do not diff a later batch against an earlier one looking for edits. There are none. What a later batch contains is new rows, new documents and new observations.
The files
Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
File
	One row is
	applications.csv
	an application revision I received in the window
	application-disclosures.csv
	one professional practice question and the applicant's answer
	declared-history.csv
	one history entry the applicant declared
	declared-credentials.csv
	one licence or certification as the applicant described it
	privilege-requests.csv
	one privilege group requested
	licence-lookup-wa.csv
	one Washington credential record from the state board's lookup
	licence-lookup-other-states.csv
	one out-of-state credential record
	certification-replies.csv
	one certifying board's reply
	verification-replies.csv
	one reply about education and training, or about an affiliation or employer
	verification-attempts.csv
	one request I sent
	peer-referees.csv
	one referee named on an application, or supplied later
	peer-reference-replies.csv
	one completed reference form that came back
	correspondence.csv
	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
	

Folder
	What is in it
	letters/
	applicants' explanation letters, withdrawals, referee substitutions, and my own written requests for missing items
	dispositions/
	the Clinical Director's recorded dispositions
	decisions/
	Credentials Committee and Executive Committee minutes extracts, and Governing Body approval records
	correspondence.csv is an index. It tells you the documents exist and where they are. It does not tell you what they say — you have to open them.
A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
Dates, blanks and columns
﻿Initial appointment — Medical Staff Office procedure
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office · Larkhollow, Washington Procedure version LARK-MSO-2026.1, in force from 2026-01-01. Approved by the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff. Maintained by the Medical Services Professional.
This procedure covers initial appointment only — a practitioner who has never held membership or privileges here. Reappointment, requests for additional privileges between appointments, credentialing by proxy, temporary privileges and emergency or disaster privileges run under separate procedures and are not described here.
Where our rules come from, and how to tell them apart
Larkhollow is a community hospital. It is not a federal facility. We adopted the verification standard work published by the Indian Health Service in its Medical Staff Credentialing and Privileging Standard Operating Procedure Manual, Version 8.0, September 2025, as our own written procedure, because it is a complete, current and publicly stated account of how the work is done.
Two kinds of sentence appear below, and each says which it is.
* Quoted from the manual, with the manual's own section number. We follow it.
* Larkhollow rule. Ours. Either the manual leaves the criterion open, or the manual's rule is tied to a federal facility and does not reach us. Where the manual says something different, or says nothing, the manual's own sentence is printed beside ours so that the difference is visible rather than buried.
Nothing below is a rule unless it is one of those two things. If you cannot find a rule here, ask the Medical Services Professional. Do not infer one from the manual, and do not invent one.
The office also runs identity verification, controlled-substance registrations, the National Practitioner Data Bank query, sanctions and exclusion lookups, life support certificates, continuing education, immunization records, liability coverage and malpractice history. Those are handled outside this procedure and are not part of the work described here.
1. Intake and completeness
We do not send the application before the offer is accepted. The manual, Section 5:
"Only after the applicant has accepted the tentative job offer can the full initial appointment application be sent to the applicant."
An application is taken up for processing only when it is complete. The manual, Section 5, opens its list with
"An application is complete and ready for import when:"
and names ten conditions, of which two govern almost everything else we do:
"a signed IHS Conditions of Application & Release is received (required to be able to conduct any verifications);"
"a request for specific privileges is received;"
Larkhollow rule. Our equivalent of that release is the Larkhollow Authorization and Release, printed inside the application. It is our own form; the manual's is a federal instrument and we do not use it. The rule it carries is the manual's and we keep it: until a signed release is on file we send no verification request of any kind. A file with no signed release cannot advance, no matter how much else is present.
Larkhollow rule — our completeness list. An application is complete when all nine hold:
1. the application is signed and dated by the applicant;
2. the Larkhollow Authorization and Release is signed and dated;
3. a request for specific privileges names at least one privilege group published in the current privilege criteria;
4. a current curriculum vitae is on file;
5. every professional practice question on the disclosure page is answered Yes or No, and every Yes carries the written explanation the form asks for;
6. the declared history runs continuously from the date the applicant finished professional school, with a written explanation for every period of 30 days or more that no entry covers;
7. at least two peer referees are named, with a working address for each;
8. every declared affiliation and employer carries a verification contact;
9. every licence and certification the applicant holds, active or inactive, is declared.
An item that is missing is requested from the applicant in writing, and the clock in the manual, Section 5, starts on the day we write:
"the LP has 30 calendar days to respond. After 30 calendar days, their application is considered incomplete and ineligible for processing."
Larkhollow rule. The 30 days run from the date on our written request, counted as calendar days, and the deadline day is included. A reply that arrives on day 30 is in time. A reply that adds or changes anything on the application arrives as a new revision of the application; we record it and keep the old one. A revision never overwrites what it replaces.
An unexplained gap does not go on a findings list. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 4:
"If the application is found to have any unexplained time period or gaps, the application will not be processed and will be returned to the applicant as incomplete."
2. Reconciliation
Before and during verification we read the curriculum vitae against the application, and then both against whatever the sources return. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
"The MSP will compare the CV/resume with the application and completed verifications and correct or resolve any discrepancies."
"There must be a follow-up of any verification discrepancies found during the application and"
"The burden of proof is on the applicant to provide all necessary verifiable information to"
And Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"If discrepancies exist, the applicant must provide a written explanation or be offered the opportunity to amend the submitted application."
Larkhollow rule — the office never picks a value. When the applicant says one thing and a source says another, we raise it and we record both. We do not decide which is right, we do not average them, and we do not quietly adopt the source's date because the source is the source. The applicant resolves it in writing or amends the application.
Larkhollow rule — a discrepancy holds its own entry and nothing else. A contested employment entry holds that entry. Every other entry on the file carries on being verified. But the file cannot be presented to the committee until the discrepancy is resolved, because presentation requires every element to be resolved (section 8 below).
Larkhollow rule — outstanding work does not stop the rest of the file. While one element of a file is outstanding, work on the other elements continues and their status is recorded; the office may hold the whole file instead only for a reason recorded in the file's action list; a file is never presented to the committee with an element outstanding.
Larkhollow rule — a revision is reconciled, not assumed. When a revision arrives, the reconciliation above runs again on what the revision says, against the curriculum vitae and against every verification already completed on the entries it touches. Dates are not the only thing a revision can move: the organization, the role, the supervisor and the verification contact all belong to the entry, and a change to any of them is a change to the entry. Section 11 says what re-opens when it does. The monitoring duty i…1383 tokens truncated…onitoring agreement, a practice limitation, a suspension, a stipulated condition or a surrender. A licence in any of those states is a finding and goes to the Clinical Director with its evidence. It is not the office's judgment whether the restriction matters.
The element's state is finding from the day the restriction is seen and stays finding on every later record of that revision, including after the Clinical Director's disposition ends the hold on the file. The disposition ends the wait; it does not turn a finding into a clean element. resolved is for an element with nothing to weigh.
Larkhollow rule — a National Provider Identifier is not a licence. It identifies a practitioner for billing. It says nothing about whether anybody is licensed. An applicant who declares an identifier in place of a licence has declared no licence.
Larkhollow rule — the cycle. An initial appointment at Larkhollow runs one year, matching the manual's Section 12:
"For IHS, initial appointments are one year long, and reappointments are two years long, regardless of accrediting body medical staff standards or medical staff bylaws."
The cycle starts on the date the appointment takes effect and ends one year later minus one day, so a cycle starting 2026-05-01 ends 2027-04-30. The Washington licence must be valid on the decision date. If it expires inside the cycle, that is not a denial and it is not a pass: it is recorded as a monitored condition with a re-verification due date set before the expiry date, and it does not block activation. If the re-verification fails, the file re-opens. The due date recorded on the condition is the licence's expiry date itself; "before" says when the re-verification must be complete, not what the recorded date is.
Check 2 — Experience and time gaps
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"At the initial appointment, relevant experience (affiliations, work history, and military) for at least the most recent five years for work history and the most recent five years for affiliation history"
"or as far back as necessary per any conflicting information or suspicious indicators—to assess current competency is verified."
Five years is a floor, not a ceiling. Conflicting information takes us further back.
Larkhollow rule — where the five years are measured from. The manual states the window and not its anchor. Ours is the date the application was first received: an entry is inside the window when any part of it falls in the five years counted back from the date the application was first received. A later revision does not move the anchor.
Element 4 defines a gap and says what is owed:
"A time gap is 30 or more days when the LP is not in school or training, in the military, teaching, working,"
"Verification of time gaps is not required, but an explanation is."
"or as far back as necessary per any conflicting information or suspicious indicators—to assess current competency is verified."
Five years is a floor, not a ceiling. Conflicting information takes us further back.
Larkhollow rule — where the five years are measured from. The manual states the window and not its anchor. Ours is the date the application was first received: an entry is inside the window when any part of it falls in the five years counted back from the date the application was first received. A later revision does not move the anchor.
Element 4 defines a gap and says what is owed:
"A time gap is 30 or more days when the LP is not in school or training, in the military, teaching, working,"
"Verification of time gaps is not required, but an explanation is."
Larkhollow rule — how the gap list is computed. The clock starts on the day after the applicant finished professional school. Every declared entry of any type covers every day from its start date to its end date inclusive; an entry with no end date runs to the export date. Overlapping entries, part-time appointments and training years are covering entries: an overlap covers, it does not create a gap. A gap is a run of 30 or more consecutive days that no entry covers. The list is recomputed from scratch whenever a revision or a verification changes a date; it is not patched.
Larkhollow rule — what the office does with a gap. We record the gap and we record the applicant's written explanation beside it. An explanation names the period it covers, and it covers a gap only when that named period runs from at or before the gap's first day to at or after the gap's last day. A gap with a written explanation covering it is marked explained. A gap with no written explanation is unexplained, and the application is returned as incomplete under the manual's sentence quoted in section 1. The office marks a gap explained on the presence of a written explanation and on nothing else. We do not read the explanation and decide whether it is good enough. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 8:
"current competency is determined by clinical leadership, not the MSP."
Larkhollow rule — the long gap. Any gap of 180 days or more is routed to the Clinical Director for a recorded disposition, whether or not it carries an explanation. The Clinical Director decides; the office supplies the gap, the explanation and the verified dates.
Check 3 — Professional education and post-graduate training
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 2:
"A qualifying degree is the degree required for the applicant's position and privileges."
"such as internship, residency, fellowship, or other organized professional training will be verified."
So: the qualifying degree, and every post-graduate training entry. The accepted sources are in attester-table.md. The admissibility rules are the ones in "What counts as a verification at all" above — the applicant may not carry the reply, and a source not on the table is raised.
The manual also states the boundary this check does not cross, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 2:
"obtaining a degree and postgraduate training does not automatically confer a license to practice"
Check 4 — Professional peer references
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 11:
"IHS policy requires the collection of at least two peer references at the initial appointment. The"
"All peer references are from a professional authority who has worked directly with the applicant within the past two years and can authoritatively speak to the applicant's character, clinical experience, and competency."
"the IHS definition of a peer includes a practitioner in the same clinical discipline."
"A peer must not be a relative, spouse, or partner."
Three disqualifiers, each independent: not worked together directly inside two years; not in the same clinical discipline; a relative, spouse or partner. A referee who fails any one of them does not count, and we find out only when the reply arrives and states the relationship.
Larkhollow rule — how each of the three is measured. The manual gives the conditions and not the arithmetic, so ours is:
* Worked together within two years is measured against the date the referee signs, because that is the day the referee attests to it. A referee whose last date working directly with the applicant is earlier than two years before their own signature date does not qualify. A blank last date means they still work together and the condition holds.
* Same clinical discipline is the discipline the referee states on the returned form against the discipline the applicant declared on the application. Both come from a fixed list.
* Relative, spouse or partner is the box the referee ticks on the returned form, read with whatever they wrote beside it.
Currency, from Section 8:
"Peer references are considered current if the reference's signature is within two years of the file presentation to the GB."
The signature date, not the date we received it. A reference can go stale while the file waits.
Larkhollow rule — when currency is measured. A reference is current when the presentation date is on or before the second anniversary of the signature date. For a file the Governing Body has decided, the presentation date is the decision date. For a file not yet decided, we measure currency against today, so that a reference about to go stale is visible before the committee meets rather than afterwards.
Larkhollow rule — the reference window. The manual states how many times to ask and does not state how long to wait. Ours: 21 calendar days per request, up to three requests. Request one goes out, request two 21 days later, request three 21 days after that. From day 64 after the first request the reference is overdue: we tell the applicant and ask for an additional referee. The original request stays open and stays outstanding; it is never closed as satisfied and never counted.
Larkhollow rule — the floor is two. Two qualifying, current references, both eligible on all three disqualifiers, both signed inside two years of the presentation date. An ineligible referee does not count towards the two even though the reply is in the file.
Larkhollow rule — an open request does not hold a met element. Once two qualifying, current references are on file, the peer-reference element is resolved. A request that is still open is carried on the action list until the file is presented and is then closed as no longer needed; it is never counted, and it does not hold the element or the file.
Check 5 — Board certification and the privileges requested
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 5:
"At the initial appointment, all active and inactive board certifications are verified."
"Verified through the certifying board."
All of them — a lapsed certificate is verified too, because what the applicant is certified in and what the applicant was once certified in are different facts and the file needs both.
On whether a certification supports a privilege, the manual gives the duty to clinical leadership:
"MSPs will check the facility's privilege criteria and conditions of employment (for IHS employees, review the position description, and for contractors, review the contract) to determine if the LP meets the board-certified/board-eligible requirements."
"The facility's clinical leadership is responsible for ensuring that the LP's board-certified or board eligibility aligns with the requested privileges."
and Section 9 says what criteria must address:
"At a minimum, privilege criteria should address the required education level, formal training requirements, and current experience."
Larkhollow rule — the criteria are published and versioned. privilege-criteria.md maps each privilege group to the certifying boards that support it and to a minimum training requirement, under a version string. Every decision record cites the criteria version it was decided under. The office applies the map; the office does not write it and does not extend it.

## Findings

Yes. Under **§9, “what makes a decision admissible,”** a presentable packet for that revision must have existed before the decision date. That condition applies to recommendations as well as approvals. The Executive Committee’s positive recommendation and the record’s statement that it reviewed a file do not replace the required readiness check. ([Procedure §8–9]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/procedure-extract.txt ), [authority roster]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/authority-roster.txt ))

The six recommendation documents follow the parser’s expected format and identify an authorized Executive Committee signatory. Their blank reason fields are permitted for `recommended`. They remain inadmissible because the packet-readiness condition is not met:

| Decision | Application | Additional readiness evidence missing |
|---|---|---|
| MEC-2026-011 | APP-2026-001 | Current employment end-date verification; accreditation evidence; peer-reference return channel |
| MEC-2026-013 | APP-2026-003 | Same |
| MEC-2026-017 | APP-2026-007 | Same |
| MEC-2026-023 | APP-2026-013 | Same |
| MEC-2026-024 | APP-2026-014 | Current employment end-date verification; accreditation evidence; a second returned reference |
| MEC-2026-034 | APP-2026-036 | Current employment end-date verification; accreditation evidence; peer-reference return channel |

These are **evidence gaps**, not findings that a school was unaccredited or that a referee used the wrong return channel. The privilege criteria require accredited education and training, but Batch 1 has no accreditation evidence. The hospital reference form requires direct return, but the export has no channel field. Neither requirement says the export must contain a dedicated structured field; the underlying evidence still must support a resolved element. I left both unresolved rather than treating missing fields as proof of compliance. ([Privilege criteria]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/privilege-criteria.txt ), [reference form]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/peer-reference-form.txt ), [export notes]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/export-notes.txt ))

The blank `verified_to` values are handled consistently with the export notes. The notes define blank `to_date` in **declared-history.csv** as current, but give no such meaning to blank `verified_to` in **verification-replies.csv**; other blanks mean the office holds no value. The ongoing employment replies therefore do not establish an end date. That is missing verification evidence, not proof that the declared history is false.

For APP-2026-014, the missing second reply is a separate outstanding item: export notes say a referee without a reply row has not replied. The other five have two replies that meet the recorded date, discipline, and relationship checks, but the direct-return channel remains unassessable.

## Code and rerun

I fixed a readiness-reporting bug in [readiness.py](/home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/credentialing/readiness.py): positive observations—such as two qualifying references or an explained gap—were listed as blockers when another issue kept the element open. They are now retained as nonblocking findings. I did not relax the accreditation, reference-channel, or source-date evidence requirements.

After the fix, all **41 revisions across 40 applications** remain not presentable and in `in-verification`. All six recommendations remain inadmissible for `packet-not-presentable-before-decision-date`; none is rejected solely because a particular structured export field is absent. No activation is authorized: Batch 1 contains no Governing Body approval.

The full suite passes: **27 tests**. No snapshots, source exports, or schema were modified. I’ll wait for your review.

content.text: The three-batch run exposed two more concrete issues: explicit withdrawal/discontinuation records were not reflected in status, and the real conditional-approval document stores conditions in a `Conditions` list rather than in the reason text. I’m fixing those parsers and the schema’s status precedence for refused decisions, then I’ll recompute the per-batch results.

The three-batch run exposed two more concrete issues: explicit withdrawal/discontinuation records were not reflected in status, and the real conditional-approval document stores conditions in a `Conditions` list rather than in the reason text. I’m fixing those parsers and the schema’s status precedence for refused decisions, then I’ll recompute the per-batch results.

const patch="*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: credentialing/readiness.py
@@
 def _parse_decisions(ledger: dict[str, Any], as_of: date) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
@@
     return out
+
+
+def _decision_conditions(d: dict[str, Any]) -> list[dict[str, str]]:
+    """Read explicitly listed condition/due pairs from a decision record."""
+    content = d.get("__content", "")
+    section = re.search(r"^\*\*Conditions:\*\*[ \t]*\r?\n(.*?)(?=^##\s|\Z)", content, re.M | re.S)
+    lines = section.group(1).splitlines() if section else []
+    result = []
+    for line in lines:
+        item = re.match(r"\s*[-*]\s+(.+?)\s+[—–-]\s+due\s+(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})\s*$", line, re.I)
+        if item and _parse_date(item.group(2)):
+            result.append({"condition": item.group(1).strip(), "due": item.group(2)})
+    # Older records may place a single explicit due-dated condition in Reason.
+    if not result:
+        for item in (d.get("reason") or "").split(";"):
+            match = re.match(r"\s*(.*?)\s+due\s+(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})\s*$", item, re.I)
+            if match and _parse_date(match.group(2)):
+                result.append({"condition": match.group(1).strip(), "due": match.group(2)})
+    return result
+
+
+def _terminal_status(ledger: dict[str, Any], app_id: str, as_of: date) -> tuple[str | None, dict[str, Any] | None]:
+    """Find explicit applicant withdrawal or roster-authorized discontinuance."""
+    for batch in ledger.get("batches", []):
+        if (_parse_date(batch.get("export_date")) or date.max) > as_of:
+            continue
+        for doc in batch.get("documents", []):
+            path, content = doc.get("path", ""), doc.get("content", "")
+            if not content:
+                continue
+            fields = _fields(content)
+            if fields.get("application") != app_id:
+                continue
+            if "/letters/" in f"/{path}" and re.search(r"\bI am withdrawing my application\b", content, re.I):
+                when = _parse_date(fields.get("date"))
+                if when and when <= as_of:
+                    return "withdrawn", _document_ref(batch, doc)
+    for disposition in _dispositions(ledger, app_id, "1", as_of):
+        content = disposition["content"]

**Applicant:** Dr. Hideo Tachibana, MD

wa_rows = [
        (batch, record) for batch, record in rows
        if record.get("filename") == "licence-lookup-wa.csv"
        and tuple(str(record.get("values", {}).get(field) or "") for field in ("lastname", "firstname", "middlename", "birthyear")) == identity
    ]
    other_rows = [
        (batch, record) for batch, record in rows
        if record.get("filename") == "licence-lookup-other-states.csv"
    ]
    matched: dict[str, list[tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]]] = {}
    for item in wa_rows:
        number = item[1]["values"].get("credentialnumber")
        if number:
            matched.setdefault(str(number), []).append(item)
    for declared_batch, declared_record in declared:
        dv = declared_record["values"]
        number = str(dv.get("number_declared") or "")
        jurisdiction = str(dv.get("jurisdiction_or_board") or "").upper()
        candidates = matched.get(number, []) if jurisdiction == "WA" else []
        if jurisdiction != "WA":
            candidates = [
                (b, r) for b, r in other_rows
                if str(r.get("values", {}).get("licence_number") or "") == number
                and str(r.get("values", {}).get("board_state") or "").upper() == jurisdiction
            ]
        if not candidates:
            element.note("licence_verification_outstanding", f"No board lookup row is linked to declared licence {number!r} ({jurisdiction}).", [_source_ref(declared_batch, declared_record)])
            continue
        for lookup_batch, lookup_record in candidates:
            lv = lookup_record["values"]
            element.cite(lookup_batch, lookup_record)
            if jurisdiction != "WA":
                verified_by = str(lv.get("verified_by") or "").casefold()
                accepted = ("board" in verified_by and "online verification" in verified_by) or "physician data center" in verified_by
                if not accepted:
                    element.note("inadmissible_license_source", f"Out-of-state licence source {lv.get('verified_by')!r} is not established as a listed board/FSMB source.", [_source_ref(lookup_batch, lookup_record)])
                    continue
            lookup_date = _parse_date(lv.get("lookup_date"))
            if lookup_date is None or lookup_date > as_of:
                element.note("invalid_license_lookup_date", f"Licence lookup date {lv.get('lookup_date')!r} is missing, invalid, or after the export date.", [_source_ref(lookup_batch, lookup_record)])
                continue
            state = str(lv.get("status") or lv.get("license_status") or "").casefold()
            action = str(lv.get("actiontaken") or lv.get("disciplinary_action") or "").casefold()
            if action not in {"", "no", "none", "none reported", "false"}:
                if action in {"yes", "pending", "true"}:
                    element.note("board_action_requires_detail", f"Board lookup indicates action ({action}); the written board detail is required before classifying the restriction.", [_source_ref(lookup_batch, lookup_record)])
                elif any(term in action for term in ("probation", "supervision", "monitoring agreement", "practice limitation", "suspend", "stipulated condition", "surrender", "restriction")):
                    element.note("licensure_finding", f"Board record states an adverse licence condition for {number!r}; preserve and route to the Clinical Director.", [_source_ref(lookup_batch, lookup_record)])
            expiration = _parse_date(lv.get("expirationdate") or lv.get("expiry_date"))
            if jurisdiction == "WA" and (state != "active" or expiration is None or expiration < as_of):
                element.note("washington_license_not_current", f"Washington lookup does not show licence {number!r} as active and unexpired on {as_of.isoformat()}.", [_source_ref(lookup_batch, lookup_record)])
            if jurisdiction == "WA" and any(term in action for term in ("yes", "pending", "stipulated", "probation", "supervision", "restriction")):
                for doc_batch, index_record, document in docs:
                    content = document.get("content", "")
                    if number in content:
                        element.cite(doc_batch, index_record, document.get("path"))
                        detail = content.casefold()
                        restrictive = any(term in detail for term in (
                            "stipulated agreement", "under supervision", "monitoring programme", "monitoring program",
                            "practice limitation", "on probation", "suspended", "surrendered", "practice restriction",
                        ))
                        negated = any(phrase in detail for phrase in (
                            "no practice restriction", "no restriction is in force", "not restricted", "no monitoring agreement",
                        ))
                        if restrictive and not negated:

Larkhollow's bylaws require a practitioner to hold one current, active, full and unrestricted licence issued by the State of Washington, which is our practice state. Every other licence the applicant holds, active or inactive, in any state, is still verified under the manual's sentence above — we verify them all; only one of them satisfies the bylaw.
Larkhollow rule — full and unrestricted. A licence is not full and unrestricted when the board's record or the board's reply shows probation, supervision, a monitoring agreement, a practice limitation, a suspension, a stipulated condition or a surrender. A licence in any of those states is a finding and goes to the Clinical Director with its evidence. It is not the office's judgment whether the restriction matters.
The element's state is finding from the day the restriction is seen and stays finding on every later record of that revision, including after the Clinical Director's disposition ends the hold on the file. The disposition ends the wait; it does not turn a finding into a clean element. resolved is for an element with nothing to weigh.
Larkhollow rule — a National Provider Identifier is not a licence. It identifies a practitioner for billing. It says nothing about whether anybody is licensed. An applicant who declares an identifier in place of a licence has declared no licence.
Larkhollow rule — the cycle. An initial appointment at Larkhollow runs one year, matching the manual's Section 12:
"For IHS, initial appointments are one year long, and reappointments are two years long, regardless of accrediting body medical staff standards or medical staff bylaws."
The cycle starts on the date the appointment takes effect and ends one year later minus one day, so a cycle starting 2026-05-01 ends 2027-04-30. The Washington licence must be valid on the decision date. If it expires inside the cycle, that is not a denial and it is not a pass: it is recorded as a monitored condition with a re-verification due date set before the expiry date, and it does not block activation. If the re-verification fails, the file re-opens. The due date recorded on the condition is the licence's expiry date itself; "before" says when the re-verification must be complete, not what the recorded date is.
Check 2 — Experience and time gaps
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"At the initial appointment, relevant experience (affiliations, work history, and military) for at least the most recent five years for work history and the most recent five years for affiliation history"
"or as far back as necessary per any conflicting information or suspicious indicators—to assess current competency is verified."
Five years is a floor, not a ceiling. Conflicting information takes us further back.
Larkhollow rule — where the five years are measured from. The manual states the window and not its anchor. Ours is the date the application was first received: an entry is inside the window when any part of it falls in the five years counted back from the date the application was first received. A later revision does not move the anchor.
Element 4 defines a gap and says what is owed:
"A time gap is 30 or more days when the LP is not in school or training, in the military, teaching, working,"
"Verification of time gaps is not required, but an explanation is."

I’ve isolated that exception to licensure; same-day evidence for other elements remains excluded. I’m rerunning the real Batch 1 audit with both fixes.

## Batch 1 audit

I ingested Batch 1 into a temporary ledger at `/tmp/project-e-stage4-batch1-ledger.json`. Ingestion reported **0 integrity issues**. The batch contains **40 applications and 41 application revisions**.

At the 2026-03-16 export date, all **41 revisions were not presentable** and had final status **`in-verification`**. The latest revision of each of the 40 applications had the same readiness and status counts.

### Recorded committee decisions

All six source documents use the parser’s expected Markdown fields. Each names the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff, the rostered chair, an application and revision, a decision date, and the `recommended` outcome. The roster authorizes that body and signatory to recommend.

| Decision | Application | Date | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| MEC-2026-011 | APP-2026-001 rev. 1 | 2026-03-10 | Rejected: packet not presentable before decision |
| MEC-2026-013 | APP-2026-003 rev. 1 | 2026-03-12 | Rejected: packet not presentable before decision |
| MEC-2026-017 | APP-2026-007 rev. 1 | 2026-03-10 | Rejected: packet not presentable before decision |
| MEC-2026-023 | APP-2026-013 rev. 1 | 2026-03-12 | Rejected: packet not presentable before decision |
| MEC-2026-024 | APP-2026-014 rev. 1 | 2026-03-10 | Rejected: packet not presentable before decision |
| MEC-2026-034 | APP-2026-036 rev. 1 | 2026-03-10 | Rejected: packet not presentable before decision |

The detailed blockers differed slightly. For five applications, the evidence included an ongoing employment verification with no source end date, no recorded accreditation proof for the required school and training, and peer-reference replies without evidence of the required direct return channel. APP-2026-014 also had only one returned reference.<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="42" />found no rejection based on evidence the written procedure says is unnecessary. The source rule and export limitations are documented in [the procedure]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/procedure-extract.txt ) and [export notes]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/export-notes.txt ).

### Activations

**None.** Batch 1 contains no Governing Body approval records. Its six decisions are committee recommendations, which cannot activate privileges. Consequently, there are no activation dates, cycle ends, privileges, or monitored conditions to report from this batch.

Batch 1 has no disposition documents, so it does not exercise disposition parsing.

## Fix made and verification

I fixed a date-handling bug in [readiness.py](/home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/credentialing/readiness.py): a later batch publication date had caused application revisions received earlier to be treated as unavailable on the decision date. The historical check now uses the application revision’s recorded `received_date`. I also applied the procedure’s exception allowing the Washington lookup on the decision date, while keeping other elements limited to evidence available before that date.

Regression tests cover both date rules. The full suite passes: **26 tests passed**, and Python compilation passed. The fix did not change Batch 1’s final decision results: each recommendation is still rejected because its packet was not presentable.

The real batch does not test approval activation or conditional-approval parsing. Condition extraction still depends on the explicit due-date wording documented in Stage 4; Batch 1 provides no conditional approval with which to validate that format. I did not create snapshots or modify source exports or the schema.

I’ll check the six recommendation records against the procedure’s admissibility conditions, then trace each readiness blocker to its export fields and documented blank meanings. I’ll preserve the evidence threshold where the procedure requires proof, and change code only if that comparison shows a factual implementation error.

The source comparison confirms that unrecorded accreditation and reference-return channel are missing evidence, not proof of a policy violation. Because the written criteria still require accredited education and direct-return references, neither can be marked verified from these exports. I did find a separate reporting bug: positive notes such as “two qualifying references” and “gap explained” were being listed as blockers when a different issue kept the element open. I’ve separated those notes from actual blockers without lowering readiness.

## Findings

Yes. Under **§9, “what makes a decision admissible,”** a presentable packet for that revision must have existed before the decision date. That condition applies to recommendations as well as approvals. The Executive Committee’s positive recommendation and the record’s statement that it reviewed a file do not replace the required readiness check. ([Procedure §8–9]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/procedure-extract.txt ), [authority roster]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/authority-roster.txt ))

The six recommendation documents follow the parser’s expected format and identify an authorized Executive Committee signatory. Their blank reason fields are permitted for `recommended`. They remain inadmissible because the packet-readiness condition is not met:

| Decision | Application | Additional readiness evidence missing |
|---|---|---|
| MEC-2026-011 | APP-2026-001 | Current employment end-date verification; accreditation evidence; peer-reference return channel |
| MEC-2026-013 | APP-2026-003 | Same |
| MEC-2026-017 | APP-2026-007 | Same |
| MEC-2026-023 | APP-2026-013 | Same |
| MEC-2026-024 | APP-2026-014 | Current employment end-date verification; accreditation evidence; a second returned reference |
| MEC-2026-034 | APP-2026-036 | Current employment end-date verification; accreditation evidence; peer-reference return channel |

These are **evidence gaps**, not findings that a school was unaccredited or that a referee used the wrong return channel. The privilege criteria require accredited education and training, but Batch 1 has no accreditation evidence. The hospital reference form requires direct return, but the export has no channel field. Neither requirement says the export must contain a dedic<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="61" />home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/peer-reference-form.txt ), [export notes]( /home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/export-notes.txt ))

The blank `verified_to` values are handled consistently with the export notes. The notes define blank `to_date` in **declared-history.csv** as current, but give no such meaning to blank `verified_to` in **verification-replies.csv**; other blanks mean the office holds no value. The ongoing employment replies therefore do not establish an end date. That is missing verification evidence, not proof that the declared history is false.

For APP-2026-014, the missing second reply is a separate outstanding item: export notes say a referee without a reply row has not replied. The other five have two replies that meet the recorded date, discipline, and relationship checks, but the direct-return channel remains unassessable.

## Code and rerun

I fixed a readiness-reporting bug in [readiness.py](/home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/credentialing/readiness.py): positive observations—such as two qualifying references or an explained gap—were listed as blockers when another issue kept the element open. They are now retained as nonblocking findings. I did not relax the accreditation, reference-channel, or source-date evidence requirements.

After the fix, all **41 revisions across 40 applications** remain not presentable and in `in-verification`. All six recommendations remain inadmissible for `packet-not-presentable-before-decision-date`; none is rejected solely because a particular structured export field is absent. No activation is authorized: Batch 1 contains no Governing Body approval.

The full suite passes: **27 tests**. No snapshots, source exports, or schema were modified. I’ll wait for your review.

I’ll process the three closed exports in order, keeping one temporary ledger outside `deliverables/`. At each export date I’ll evaluate every application revision present so far, so later evidence and decisions won’t leak into earlier results. I’ll report the counts by batch and inspect any decision, disposition, or status changes that look inconsistent with the source records or written rules.

The three-batch run exposed two more concrete issues: explicit withdrawal/discontinuation records were not reflected in status, and the real conditional-approval document stores conditions in a `Conditions` list rather than in the reason text. I’m fixing those parsers and the schema’s status precedence for refused decisions, then I’ll recompute the per-batch results.

A further disposition check found two behavior bugs. The Batch 3 Clinical Director disposition for APP-2026-015 discusses the official board action, but the evaluator kept a “board detail required” hold even after that detail was present. Also, an APP-2026-027 disposition to offer an amendment was being treated as clearing an eligibility question even though the unsupported request had not changed. I’m correcting both so recorded evidence can clear only the hold the written procedure allows.

office/procedure-extract.txt:121:Larkhollow rule — when currency is measured. A reference is current when the presentation date is on or before the second anniversary of the signature date. For a file the Governing Body has decided, the presentation date is the decision date. For a file not yet decided, we measure currency against today, so that a reference about to go stale is visible before the committee meets rather than afterwards.
office/procedure-extract.txt:122:Larkhollow rule — the reference window. The manual states how many times to ask and does not state how long to wait. Ours: 21 calendar days per request, up to three requests. Request one goes out, request two 21 days later, request three 21 days after that. From day 64 after the first request the reference is overdue: we tell the applicant and ask for an additional referee. The original request stays open and stays outstanding; it is never closed as satisfied and never counted.
office/procedure-extract.txt:123:Larkhollow rule — the floor is two. Two qualifying, current references, both eligible on all three disqualifiers, both signed inside two years of the presentation date. An ineligible referee does not count towards the two even though the reply is in the file.
office/procedure-extract.txt:124:Larkhollow rule — an open request does not hold a met element. Once two qualifying, current references are on file, the peer-reference element is resolved. A request that is still open is carried on the action list until the file is presented and is then closed as no longer needed; it is never counted, and it does not hold the element or the file.

office/procedure-extract.txt:178:Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. The anchor is the date revision 1 arrived, not the date of the current revision, so a later revision does not by itself void every verification already completed — what a revision invalidates is decided entry by entry, by reading what the revision actually changed. Peer references carry the additional two-year signature rule in check 4, which is stricter and wins where the two disagree.
office/procedure-extract.txt:183:Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. A refused decision record does not undo it, and a withdrawn or discontinued file keeps the readiness its revision had: the office records what was ready, whatever the file did next. Only an element re-opening or a new revision changes it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:185:The medical staff recommends; the Governing Body approves. The manual, Section 1:
office/procedure-extract.txt:188:"proposes a recommendation through the clinical director (CD) and the chief executive officer (CEO) or their designee to the Governing Body"
office/procedure-extract.txt:190:"The GB or a delegated GB committee retains the final authority to grant, renew, or deny privileges after considering the recommendations of the medical staff"
office/procedure-extract.txt:192:"All signatories should utilize a "recommend" selection, with only the Chair of the GB or their designee using the "approval" selection."
office/procedure-extract.txt:193:A recommendation is not an approval. A record from the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff that carries the word "approved" is still a recommendation, because those bodies cannot approve. Only the Governing Body chair, or the designee named in authority-roster.md, records an approval.
office/procedure-extract.txt:199:5. the outcome is one of approved, approved-with-conditions, deferred-pending-information, denied, recommended, not recommended, and every outcome other than a plain approval carries a reason.
office/procedure-extract.txt:202:Larkhollow rule — two decisions for one revision. A second decision for the same application revision is admissible only when it names the earlier decision it supersedes. Without that reference it is a duplicate, it is inadmissible, and it is raised to the Medical Services Professional. The first decision continues to stand.
office/procedure-extract.txt:203:Larkhollow rule — which outcomes carry a reason, and what counts as a second decision. recommended is the positive outcome of a body that cannot approve (the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff); like a plain approval it carries no reason, while not recommended carries one, as do approval-with-conditions, deferral and denial. The two-decisions rule above applies to a second decision of the same body for the same revision: a recommendation followed by the Governing Body's decision on the same revision is the normal sequence, not a duplicate, and a second recommendation is never a duplicate — so in practice it is a second Governing Body decision for the same revision that must name the earlier one it supersedes.
office/procedure-extract.txt:213:Larkhollow rule — approve with conditions. An approval with conditions activates the approved privilege groups on the normal rule above, and records each condition as a monitored condition with its own due date. A condition is satisfied only by a record naming it. A condition still unmet on its due date becomes a finding to the Clinical Director.
office/procedure-extract.txt:214:Monitored conditions do not block activation. A licence expiring inside the cycle, and a condition attached to an approval, are both tracked to their due dates while the privileges run.

I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
The export date is the clock
Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
A batch is closed. It never changes.
I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
So: do not diff a later batch against an earlier one looking for edits. There are none. What a later batch contains is new rows, new documents and new observations.
The files
Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
File
	One row is
	applications.csv
	an application revision I received in the window
	application-disclosures.csv
	one professional practice question and the applicant's answer
	declared-history.csv
	one history entry the applicant declared
	declared-credentials.csv
	one licence or certification as the applicant described it
	privilege-requests.csv
	one privilege group requested
	licence-lookup-wa.csv
	one Washington credential record from the state board's lookup
	licence-lookup-other-states.csv
	one out-of-state credential record
	certification-replies.csv
	one certifying board's reply
	verification-replies.csv
	one reply about education and training, or about an affiliation or employer
	verification-attempts.csv
	one request I sent
	peer-referees.csv
	one referee named on an application, or supplied later
	peer-reference-replies.csv
	one completed reference form that came back
	correspondence.csv
	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
	

Folder
	What is in it
	letters/
	applicants' explanation letters, withdrawals, referee substitutions, and my own written requests for missing items
	dispositions/
	the Clinical Director's recorded dispositions
	decisions/
	Credentials Committee and Executive Committee minutes extracts, and Governing Body approval records
	correspondence.csv is an index. It tells you the documents exist and where they are. It does not tell you what they say — you have to open them.
A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
Dates, blanks and columns
* Dates are YYYY-MM-DD. Always. A date range is inclusive at both ends: an entry from_date 2022-01-01, to_date 2022-12-31 covers the 1st of January and the 31st of December. An expiry date is the last day the credential is valid.
* An empty cell means I hold no value for that field. It does not mean zero, it does not mean "no", and it does not mean the answer is unknown-but-probably-fine. Two blanks carry a specific meaning and you should learn them:
   * a blank to_date in declared-history.csv means the entry is current, running to the export date — not that the end date is missing;
   * a blank expiry_date in certification-replies.csv means the certificate does not expire — some older certificates are time-unlimited.
* No money appears anywhere. We do not record fees, salaries or contract values in the credentialing file.
* Files are UTF-8 with Unix line endings. Values are quoted only when they contain a comma.
The three joins that matter
1. Everything on the applicant side joins on application_id, and on revision where the fact belongs to a revision. Entries, credentials, privilege requests and disclosures all restate on each revision, so always filter to the revision you are working.
2. The Washington board export carries no practitioner identifier. It never has. I join it to an application on lastname, firstname, middlename and birthyear. I have checked that no two rows in any one export share those four values, so the join gives you at most one row. An applicant with no row in that file holds no Washington credential. The absence is the answer, not a data problem.
3. A referee with no row in peer-reference-replies.csv has not replied. Silence produces no record. You can see it only by looking at the requests in verification-attempts.csv and finding no reply against them.
The Washington export's own columns
I pass that file through as the board publishes it and add one column. The board's twelve are credentialnumber, credentialtype, status, firstissuedate, lastissuedate, expirationdate, ceduedate, actiontaken, birthyear, firstname, middlename, lastname. Mine is lookup_date — the day I ran the lookup. It is my own act, not a source's reply, so the usability window is not applied to it.
Two of the board's columns are easy to misread:
* ceduedate is a continuing-education due date. We do not use it. Continuing education is handled outside this procedure and it has nothing to do with whether a licence is valid.
* actiontaken says the board has acted. It does not say what the action was. For that you need the board's written reply, which arrives as a document, not in this file. A Yes here is a reason to go and read; it is not a conclusion.
The first export carries the board's whole file for our county — 435 rows — so you can see what an ordinary population looks like. The second and third carry only a re-lookup of the practitioners whose files are open, because that is all I re-run.
How often anything is actually wrong
I want to say this plainly, because a small sample of credentialing files can leave the wrong impression.
In the board's population, action against a credential is rare. In the 435-row export you have: 431 rows say No, 3 say Yes, and 1 says Pending. That is 0.69% Yes and 0.23% Pending, and it is the shape of the real thing — the overwhelming majority of licensed practitioners have a clean board record, and any tool that expects otherwise will be wrong almost every time it fires.
The applicants in these batches are a different matter, and deliberately so. This is a teaching set. I have put every situation the procedure has a rule for into these three exports on purpose, so the run has something to exercise: a restricted licence, an unexplained gap, a school that closed, a referee who never answers, a certificate that lapsed, a decision against the wrong revision. A real nine weeks of intake would be far quieter than this. Do not read the applicant set as a base rate. Read it as a checklist that happens to be shaped like a caseload.
The clean files are genuinely clean. If your tool raises something on one of them, it is your tool.
What I do not export
My own queue, my own statuses and my own conclusions. This export is the evidence, not my reading of it. What is complete, what is outstanding, what is presentable and what is owed to whom is the work — it is not in the folder, and it should not be.
Referee addresses. The export carries no address column for peer referees. The working-address half of completeness condition 7 is checked by my office outside the export, so a run assesses condition 7 on the named referees alone and records the address check as not assessable from the export — neither met nor failed.and Section 8, on how long a verification stays good:
"Most of these verifications are required by accrediting organizations to be verified AT the time of appointment, the time between when the application is received and when it's reviewed."
The manual gave a fixed number once and removed it: its own change log for Version 5.0 records "Section 8: Removed 120-day expiration of primary source verifications."
Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. The anchor is the date revision 1 arrived, not the date of the current revision, so a later revision does not by itself void every verification already completed — what a revision invalidates is decided entry by entry, by reading what the revision actually changed. Peer references carry the additional two-year signature rule in check 4, which is stricter and wins where the two disagree.
Larkhollow rule — the board lookup and the window. A board lookup is the office's own check of the state board's public record on a day of the office's choosing, not a reply from a source, so the usability window is not applied to it: a lookup run on the decision day is usable for that decision. The date a packet became presentable is the date the last verification reply it needed was received; the lookup does not set it.
Larkhollow rule — what makes a packet presentable. Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is computed from the element statuses, not from anybody's recollection that the file looked finished.
For readiness, resolved means the element has nothing left to verify. An element carrying a finding is resolved in that sense once its evidence is with the Clinical Director — a licensure finding once the Clinical Director's disposition is on file, a certification finding on part of the request at once — and the packet is presented with the finding on it. An eligibility question, a gap awaiting the Clinical Director's disposition, an open discrepancy, an item returned to the applicant and a high-risk finding without its disposition are not resolved: while any of them stands, the packet is not presentable.
A packet is a statement about one revision at one moment. If any element re-opens, readiness for that revision is gone, and the earlier readiness record stays in the file as history.
Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. A refused decision record does not undo it, and a withdrawn or discontinued file keeps the readiness its revision had: the office records what was ready, whatever the file did next. Only an element re-opening or a new revision changes it.
9. The committee protocol
The medical staff recommends; the Governing Body approves. The manual, Section 1:
"The Governing Body has the authority to grant, modify, or deny medical staff membership and clinical privileges to LPs"
and the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff
"proposes a recommendation through the clinical director (CD) and the chief executive officer (CEO) or their designee to the Governing Body"
Section 7:
"The GB or a delegated GB committee retains the final authority to grant, renew, or deny privileges after considering the recommendations of the medical staff"
Section 12, on who may record what:
"All signatories should utilize a "recommend" selection, with only the Chair of the GB or their designee using the "approval" selection."
A recommendation is not an approval. A record from the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff that carries the word "approved" is still a recommendation, because those bodies cannot approve. Only the Governing Body chair, or the designee named in authority-roster.md, records an approval.
Larkhollow rule — what makes a decision admissible. All five, checked against the roster and the packet and never against the record's own claim:
1. the body is one that may record that outcome;
2. the signatory held the named role on the decision date, per authority-roster.md;
3. the decision names the same applicant and the same application revision as the presentable packet;
4. a presentable packet existed for that revision before the decision date;
5. the outcome is one of approved, approved-with-conditions, deferred-pending-information, denied, recommended, not recommended, and every outcome other than a plain approval carries a reason.
A decision that fails any of these is not a decision. It is recorded as received, raised to the Medical Services Professional, and nothing activates on it.
Larkhollow rule — a decision against a superseded revision. It does not authorize the current revision. It stays in the file as history against the revision it named, and it is never deleted.
Larkhollow rule — two decisions for one revision. A second decision for the same application revision is admissible only when it names the earlier decision it supersedes. Without that reference it is a duplicate, it is inadmissible, and it is raised to the Medical Services Professional. The first decision continues to stand.
Larkhollow rule — which outcomes carry a reason, and what counts as a second decision. recommended is the positive outcome of a body that cannot approve (the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff); like a plain approval it carries no reason, while not recommended carries one, as do approval-with-conditions, deferral and denial. Larkhollow rule — deferral. A deferral names the information it waits for. The office chases exactly that, and the file does not advance while it waits.
10. Activation and the appointment cycle
The manual, Section 5:
"The provider cannot provide patient care services until the practitioner has been approved for their next appointment and privilege cycle."
and Section 15:
"The GB needs to approve a provider's privileges and/or appointment on or before the"
expiry date, to prevent a lapse; and a later start date is permitted when the body records it:
"Yes, if the GB makes the notation in their final notes when they sign off on the signature pages in Virtual Committee."
