On an admitted Governing Body approval, the office records the appointment and activates exactly the privilege groups named in the decision — never more, and never a group that was requested but not granted. Privileges become active on the effective date the decision records, or on the decision date when the decision records no separate effective date. Nothing is active before that day. "The MSP must verify all expirables upon expiration and place the documentation in the file."
"must continue monitoring expirables even during the review process and always provide the most current information"

I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
The export date is the clock
Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
A batch is closed. It never changes.
I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
So: do not diff a later batch against an earlier one looking for edits. There are none. What a later batch contains is new rows, new documents and new observations.
The files
Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
File
	One row is
	applications.csv
	an application revision I received in the window
	application-disclosures.csv
	one professional practice question and the applicant's answer
	declared-history.csv
	one history entry the applicant declared
	declared-credentials.csv
	one licence or certification as the applicant described it
	privilege-requests.csv
	one privilege group requested
	licence-lookup-wa.csv
	one Washington credential record from the state board's lookup
	licence-lookup-other-states.csv
	one out-of-state credential record
	certification-replies.csv
	one certifying board's reply
	verification-replies.csv
	one reply about education and training, or about an affiliation or employer
	verification-attempts.csv
	one request I sent
	peer-referees.csv
	one referee named on an application, or supplied later
	peer-reference-replies.csv
	one completed reference form that came back
	correspondence.csv
	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
	

Folder
	What is in it
	letters/
	applicants' explanation letters, withdrawals, referee substitutions, and my own written requests for missing items
	dispositions/
	the Clinical Director's recorded dispositions
	decisions/
	Credentials Committee and Executive Committee minutes extracts, and Governing Body approval records
	correspondence.csv is an index. It tells you the documents exist and where they are. It does not tell you what they say — you have to open them.
A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
Dates, blanks and columns
* Dates are YYYY-MM-DD. Always. A date range is inclusive at both ends: an entry from_date 2022-01-01, to_date 2022-12-31 covers the 1st of January and the 31st of December. An expiry date is the last day the credential is valid.
* An empty cell means I hold no value for that field. It does not mean zero, it does not mean "no", and it does not mean the answer is unknown-but-probably-fine. Two blanks carry a specific meaning and you should learn them:
   * a blank to_date in declared-history.csv means the entry is current, running to the export date — not that the end date is missing;
   * a blank expiry_date in certification-replies.csv means the certificate does not expire — some older certificates are time-unlimited.
* No money appears anywhere. We do not record fees, salaries or contract values in the credentialing file.
* Files are UTF-8 with Unix line endings. Values are quoted only when they contain a comma.
The three joins that matter
1. Everything on the applicant side joins on application_id, and on revision where the fact belongs to a revision. Entries, credentials, privilege requests and disclosures all restate on each revision, so always filter to the revision you are working.
2. The Washington board export carries no practitioner identifier. It never has. I join it to an application on lastname, firstname, middlename and birthyear. I have checked that no two rows in any one export share those four values, so the join gives you at most one row. An applicant with no row in that file holds no Washington credential. The absence is the answer, not a data problem.
3. A referee with no row in peer-reference-replies.csv has not replied. Silence produces no record. You can see it only by looking at the requests in verification-attempts.csv and finding no reply against them.

Mine is lookup_date — the day I ran the lookup. It is my own act, not a source's reply, so the usability window is not applied to it.

A board lookup is the office's own check of the state board's public record on a day of the office's choosing, not a reply from a source, so the usability window is not applied to it: a lookup run on the decision day is usable for that decision. The date a packet became presentable is the date the last verification reply it needed was received; the lookup does not set it.

Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is computed from the element statuses, not from anybody's recollection that the file looked finished.
For readiness, resolved means the element has nothing left to verify. A real nine weeks of intake would be far quieter than this. Do not read the applicant set as a base rate. Read it as a checklist that happens to be shaped like a caseload.
The clean files are genuinely clean. If your tool raises something on one of them, it is your tool.
What I do not export
My own queue, my own statuses and my own conclusions. This export is the evidence, not my reading of it. What is complete, what is outstanding, what is presentable and what is owed to whom is the work — it is not in the folder, and it should not be.
Referee addresses. The export carries no address column for peer referees. The working-address half of completeness condition 7 is checked by my office outside the export, so a run assesses condition 7 on the named referees alone and records the address check as not assessable from the export — neither met nor failed.and Section 8, on how long a verification stays good:
"Most of these verifications are required by accrediting organizations to be verified AT the time of appointment, the time between when the application is received and when it's reviewed."
The manual gave a fixed number once and removed it: its own change log for Version 5.0 records "Section 8: Removed 120-day expiration of primary source verifications."
Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. The anchor is the date revision 1 arrived, not the date of the current revision, so a later revision does not by itself void every verification already completed — what a revision invalidates is decided entry by entry, by reading what the revision actually changed. Peer references carry the additional two-year signature rule in check 4, which is stricter and wins where the two disagree.
Larkhollow rule — the board lookup and the window. A board lookup is the office's own check of the state board's public record on a day of the office's choosing, not a reply from a source, so the usability window is not applied to it: a lookup run on the decision day is usable for that decision. The date a packet became presentable is the date the last verification reply it needed was received; the lookup does not set it.
Larkhollow rule — what makes a packet presentable. Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is computed from the element statuses, not from anybody's recollection that the file looked finished.
For readiness, resolved means the element has nothing left to verify. An element carrying a finding is resolved in that sense once its evidence is with the Clinical Director — a licensure finding once the Clinical Director's disposition is on file, a certification finding on part of the request at once — and the packet is presented with the finding on it. An eligibility question, a gap awaiting the Clinical Director's disposition, an open discrepancy, an item returned to the applicant and a high-risk finding without its disposition are not resolved: while any of them stands, the packet is not presentable.
A packet is a statement about one revision at one moment. If any element re-opens, readiness for that revision is gone, and the earlier readiness record stays in the file as history.
Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. A refused decision record does not undo it, and a withdrawn or discontinued file keeps the readiness its revision had: the office records what was ready, whatever the file did next. Only an element re-opening or a new revision changes it.
9. The committee protocol
The medical staff recommends; the Governing Body approves. The manual, Section 1:
"The Governing Body has the authority to grant, modify, or deny medical staff membership and clinical privileges to LPs"
and the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff
"proposes a recommendation through the clinical director (CD) and the chief executive officer (CEO) or their designee to the Governing Body"
Section 7:
"The GB or a delegated GB committee retains the final authority to grant, renew, or deny privileges after considering the recommendations of the medical staff"
Section 12, on who may record what:
"All signatories should utilize a "recommend" selection, with only the Chair of the GB or their designee using the "approval" selection."
A recommendation is not an approval. A record from the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff that carries the word "approved" is still a recommendation, because those bodies cannot approve. Only the Governing Body chair, or the designee named in authority-roster.md, records an approval.
Larkhollow rule — what makes a decision admissible. All five, checked against the roster and the packet and never against the record's own claim:
1. the body is one that may record that outcome;
2. the signatory held the named role on the decision date, per authority-roster.md;
3. the decision names the same applicant and the same application revision as the presentable packet;
4. a presentable packet existed for that revision before the decision date;
5. the outcome is one of approved, approved-with-conditions, deferred-pending-information, denied, recommended, not recommended, and every outcome other than a plain approval carries a reason.
A decision that fails any of these is not a decision. It is recorded as received, raised to the Medical Services Professional, and nothing activates on it.
Larkhollow rule — a decision against a superseded revision. It does not authorize the current revision. It stays in the file as history against the revision it named, and it is never deleted.
Larkhollow rule — two decisions for one revision. A second decision for the same application revision is admissible only when it names the earlier decision it supersedes. Without that reference it is a duplicate, it is inadmissible, and it is raised to the Medical Services Professional. The first decision continues to stand.
Larkhollow rule — which outcomes carry a reason, and what counts as a second decision. recommended is the positive outcome of a body that cannot approve (the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff); like a plain approval it carries no reason, while not recommended carries one, as do approval-with-conditions, deferral and denial. The two-decisions rule above applies to a second decision of the same body for the same revision: a recommendation followed by the Governing Body's decision on the same revision is the normal sequence, not a duplicate, and a second recommendation is never a duplicate — so in practice it is a second Governing Body decision for the same revision that must name the earlier one it supersedes.
Larkhollow rule — deferral. A deferral names the information it waits for. The office chases exactly that, and the file does not advance while it waits.
10. Activation and the appointment cycle
The manual, Section 5:
"The provider cannot provide patient care services until the practitioner has been approved for their next appointment and privilege cycle."
and Section 15:
"The GB needs to approve a provider's privileges and/or appointment on or before the"
expiry date, to prevent a lapse; and a later start date is permitted when the body records it:
"Yes, if the GB makes the notation in their final notes when they sign off on the signature pages in Virtual Committee."
Larkhollow rule — activation. On an admitted Governing Body approval, the office records the appointment and activates exactly the privilege groups named in the decision — never more, and never a group that was requested but not granted. Privileges become active on the effective date the decision records, or on the decision date when the decision records no separate effective date. Nothing is active before that day. The cycle end is computed as in check 1.
Larkhollow rule — approve with conditions. An approval with conditions activates the approved privilege groups on the normal rule above, and records each condition as a monitored condition with its own due date. A condition is satisfied only by a record naming it. A condition still unmet on its due date becomes a finding to the Clinical Director.
Monitored conditions do not block activation. A licence expiring inside the cycle, and a condition attached to an approval, are both tracked to their due dates while the privileges run.
11. Re-entry: when something lands on work already done
The manual, Section 15:
"The MSP must verify all expirables upon expiration and place the documentation in the file."
"must continue monitoring expirables even during the review process and always provide the most current information"

Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office Roster version LARK-AUTH-2026.1, effective 2026-01-01. Maintained by the Medical Staff Office from the Governing Body's appointment records.
Every decision record is validated against this roster. A record that names a signatory and a role is checked here: did that person hold that role on the decision date, and may the body they signed for record that outcome. A record's own claim of authority is not evidence of it.

## Three-batch run

I ingested the exports in order into a temporary ledger at `/tmp/project-e-final-audit-8f035ria/evidence-ledger.json`. At each export date, I evaluated every application revision known by that date. The ledger accumulated earlier evidence, revisions, and decisions; later batches did not change the earlier as-of results.

| Export | New CSV records | New documents: letters / decisions / dispositions | Integrity issues | Applications / revisions known |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Batch 1 — 2026-03-16 | 1,631 | 9 / 6 / 0 (15 total) | 0 | 40 / 41 |
| Batch 2 — 2026-04-20 | 214 | 8 / 29 / 4 (41 total) | 0 | 40 / 45 |
| Batch 3 — 2026-05-18 | 100 | 4 / 21 / 1 (26 total) | 0 | 40 / 46 |

All revisions were assessed **not presentable** at each export date.

| Export | Status counts across all revisions | Status counts for latest revision per application |
|---|---|---|
| Batch 1 | 6 decision-inadmissible; 35 in-verification | 6 decision-inadmissible; 34 in-verification |
| Batch 2 | 27 decision-inadmissible; 16 in-verification; 1 withdrawn; 1 discontinued | 25 decision-inadmissible; 13 in-verification; 1 withdrawn; 1 discontinued |
| Batch 3 | 30 decision-inadmissible; 14 in-verification; 1 withdrawn; 1 discontinued | 27 decision-inadmissible; 11 in-verification; 1 withdrawn; 1 discontinued |

The withdrawn and discontinued files remain in the caseload, as the export notes require. The all-revision counts retain earlier revisions; latest-revision counts show only the current revision of each application.

## Committee decisions

There were **56 distinct decision records** by Batch 3. **None was admitted**, and there were **no activations**.

The evaluator’s primary reason was `packet-not-presentable-before-decision-date` for **55 decisions**. The written procedure requires a presentable packet for the named revision before a decision, including recommendations, deferrals, and denials. The remaining decision, MEC-2026-036, was rejected as `body-or-outcome-not-authorized`: the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff recorded “approved,” an outcome reserved to the Governing Body. These checks follow Procedure §9 and the [authority roster](</home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/authority-roster.txt>).

Here are all decisions, grouped by the export in which they first appeared. Each entry gives decision ID, application/revision, and recorded outcome; the group-level reason above applies unless noted.

## Activations, conditions, and source comparison

There were **no activations**, so there are no active privilege groups or cycle dates to report. The parser did recover both conditions from GBD-2026-039’s actual `Conditions` section:

- Washington licence re-verification before expiry on 2026-12-31; due 2026-11-30.
- Clinical Director’s written concurrence on the 2021 practice-gap explanation; due 2026-06-30.

They remain recorded with the decision, but an inadmissible approval does not activate privileges or create active monitored conditions.

The packet holds largely reflect required evidence that cannot be established from the exports, including accreditation support and direct-return reference evidence. I treated those as **unassessable/missing evidence**, not as proven policy violations, and did not mark the elements verified. This follows Procedure §8’s presentability criteria while respecting the export notes’ blank-field semantics: only the specified blanks have special meanings; a blank verification-reply end date is not evidence that an affiliation is current. The [export notes](</home/maxg/practitioner-credentialing/office/export-notes.txt>) also say that absent reference replies represent silence, not completion.

The Batch 2 withdrawal and discontinuance records were recognized as terminal statuses. The actual conditional-approval format and the Batch 3 Clinical Director disposition were also parsed; the latter clears the applicable hold while preserving the historical licensure finding. These changes do not invent human decisions or missing proof.

I fixed the condition-list parser, withdrawal/discontinuance status handling, decision-status precedence, disposition handling, and readiness reporting so positive evidence notes are not mislabeled as blockers. I added regression coverage for those issues and the board-detail disposition case.

The test suite passes: **31 tests, all successful**. The temporary ledger and summary are outside `deliverables/`. I did not create snapshots, modify source exports or the snapshot schema, or commit anything.

office/export-notes.txt:1:How this office exports its credentialing records
office/export-notes.txt:2:Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office A note from the Medical Services Professional to whoever automates the initial-appointment file. Written 2026-03-16, alongside the first export.
office/export-notes.txt:3:I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
office/export-notes.txt:4:The export date is the clock
office/export-notes.txt:5:Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
office/export-notes.txt:6:The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
office/export-notes.txt:7:The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
office/export-notes.txt:9:I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
office/export-notes.txt:12:Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
office/export-notes.txt:31:	verification-replies.csv
office/export-notes.txt:33:	verification-attempts.csv
office/export-notes.txt:37:	peer-reference-replies.csv
office/export-notes.txt:38:	one completed reference form that came back
office/export-notes.txt:40:	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
office/export-notes.txt:49:	decisions/
office/export-notes.txt:52:A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
office/export-notes.txt:53:Dates, blanks and columns
office/export-notes.txt:55:* An empty cell means I hold no value for that field. It does not mean zero, it does not mean "no", and it does not mean the answer is unknown-but-probably-fine. Two blanks carry a specific meaning and you should learn them:
office/export-notes.txt:56:   * a blank to_date in declared-history.csv means the entry is current, running to the export date — not that the end date is missing;
office/export-notes.txt:57:   * a blank expiry_date in certification-replies.csv means the certificate does not expire — some older certificates are time-unlimited.
office/export-notes.txt:62:2. The Washington board export carries no practitioner identifier. It never has. I join it to an application on lastname, firstname, middlename and birthyear. I have checked that no two rows in any one export share those four values, so the join gives you at most one row. An applicant with no row in that file holds no Washington credential. The absence is the answer, not a data problem.
office/export-notes.txt:63:3. A referee with no row in peer-reference-replies.csv has not replied. Silence produces no record. You can see it only by looking at the requests in verification-attempts.csv and finding no reply against them.
office/export-notes.txt:64:The Washington export's own columns
office/export-notes.txt:69:The first export carries the board's whole file for our county — 435 rows — so you can see what an ordinary population looks like. The second and third carry only a re-lookup of the practitioners whose files are open, because that is all I re-run.
office/export-notes.txt:72:In the board's population, action against a credential is rare. In the 435-row export you have: 431 rows say No, 3 say Yes, and 1 says Pending. That is 0.69% Yes and 0.23% Pending, and it is the shape of the real thing — the overwhelming majority of licensed practitioners have a clean board record, and any tool that expects otherwise will be wrong almost every time it fires.
office/export-notes.txt:73:The applicants in these batches are a different matter, and deliberately so. This is a teaching set. I have put every situation the procedure has a rule for into these three exports on purpose, so the run has something to exercise: a restricted licence, an unexplained gap, a school that closed, a referee who never answers, a certificate that lapsed, a decision against the wrong revision. A real nine weeks of intake would be far quieter than this. Do not read the applicant set as a base rate. Read it as a checklist that happens to be shaped like a caseload.
office/export-notes.txt:75:What I do not export
office/export-notes.txt:76:My own queue, my own statuses and my own conclusions. This export is the evidence, not my reading of it. What is complete, what is outstanding, what is presentable and what is owed to whom is the work — it is not in the folder, and it should not be.
office/export-notes.txt:77:Referee addresses. The export carries no address column for peer referees. The working-address half of completeness condition 7 is checked by my office outside the export, so a run assesses condition 7 on the named referees alone and records the address check as not assessable from the export — neither met nor failed.

office/procedure-extract.txt:5:Larkhollow is a community hospital. It is not a federal facility. We adopted the verification standard work published by the Indian Health Service in its Medical Staff Credentialing and Privileging Standard Operating Procedure Manual, Version 8.0, September 2025, as our own written procedure, because it is a complete, current and publicly stated account of how the work is done.
office/procedure-extract.txt:10:The office also runs identity verification, controlled-substance registrations, the National Practitioner Data Bank query, sanctions and exclusion lookups, life support certificates, continuing education, immunization records, liability coverage and malpractice history. Those are handled outside this procedure and are not part of the work described here.
office/procedure-extract.txt:17:"a signed IHS Conditions of Application & Release is received (required to be able to conduct any verifications);"
office/procedure-extract.txt:19:Larkhollow rule. Our equivalent of that release is the Larkhollow Authorization and Release, printed inside the application. It is our own form; the manual's is a federal instrument and we do not use it. The rule it carries is the manual's and we keep it: until a signed release is on file we send no verification request of any kind. A file with no signed release cannot advance, no matter how much else is present.
office/procedure-extract.txt:27:7. at least two peer referees are named, with a working address for each;
office/procedure-extract.txt:28:8. every declared affiliation and employer carries a verification contact;
office/procedure-extract.txt:36:Before and during verification we read the curriculum vitae against the application, and then both against whatever the sources return. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
office/procedure-extract.txt:37:"The MSP will compare the CV/resume with the application and completed verifications and correct or resolve any discrepancies."
office/procedure-extract.txt:38:"There must be a follow-up of any verification discrepancies found during the application and"
office/procedure-extract.txt:45:Larkhollow rule — a revision is reconciled, not assumed. When a revision arrives, the reconciliation above runs again on what the revision says, against the curriculum vitae and against every verification already completed on the entries it touches. Dates are not the only thing a revision can move: the organization, the role, the supervisor and the verification contact all belong to the entry, and a change to any of them is a change to the entry. Section 11 says what re-opens when it does. The monitoring duty in section 11 runs alongside it and does not pause while a file waits.
office/procedure-extract.txt:47:Six elements are verified in this procedure: licensure, experience, time gaps, professional education and post-graduate training, board certification, and professional peer references. The manual numbers seventeen essential credentialing elements in Section 6, Subsection 4. Of the other eleven, nine are handled by the office outside this procedure, as stated above; current competency is the clinical leadership's, not the office's; and the manual's conditions-and-release form is replaced by our own Authorization and Release, which is part of intake in this procedure.
office/procedure-extract.txt:48:What counts as a verification at all
office/procedure-extract.txt:49:The manual, Section 1, defines primary source verification as
office/procedure-extract.txt:52:"Primary source verifications received directly from the applicant cannot be used."
office/procedure-extract.txt:53:"Copies of a diploma, license, registration, etc., in place of verifications are unacceptable."
office/procedure-extract.txt:54:A reply that reached us through the applicant is not a verification, however genuine the document looks, however clear the letterhead, however real the registrar's signature. It goes in the file as received and the request stays open.
office/procedure-extract.txt:56:"etc., as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for education and training verifications"
office/procedure-extract.txt:58:"or other nationally recognized certifying body, as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for board certification verifications"
office/procedure-extract.txt:61:"If completing primary or DES verifications is impossible, such as when an educational institution or residency program has closed, secondary source verifications may be used."
office/procedure-extract.txt:62:"When a primary or designated equivalent source cannot be obtained, the applicant's recent affiliations should be contacted to discover how they obtained the verification."
office/procedure-extract.txt:67:"Each attempt, including whom it was attempted to verify with, the date of request, verification methods, and any additional comments, is documented in the Notes section of the entry."
office/procedure-extract.txt:70:"If the affiliation is unwilling to complete the verification or is non-responsive after 3 attempts, this should be noted as a red flag."
office/procedure-extract.txt:85:"For IHS, initial appointments are one year long, and reappointments are two years long, regardless of accrediting body medical staff standards or medical staff bylaws."
office/procedure-extract.txt:86:The cycle starts on the date the appointment takes effect and ends one year later minus one day, so a cycle starting 2026-05-01 ends 2027-04-30. The Washington licence must be valid on the decision date. If it expires inside the cycle, that is not a denial and it is not a pass: it is recorded as a monitored condition with a re-verification due date set before the expiry date, and it does not block activation. If the re-verification fails, the file re-opens. The due date recorded on the condition is the licence's expiry date itself; "before" says when the re-verification must be complete, not what the recorded date is.
office/procedure-extract.txt:96:Larkhollow rule — how the gap list is computed. The clock starts on the day after the applicant finished professional school. Every declared entry of any type covers every day from its start date to its end date inclusive; an entry with no end date runs to the export date. Overlapping entries, part-time appointments and training years are covering entries: an overlap covers, it does not create a gap. A gap is a run of 30 or more consecutive days that no entry covers. The list is recomputed from scratch whenever a revision or a verification changes a date; it is not patched.
office/procedure-extract.txt:104:So: the qualifying degree, and every post-graduate training entry. The accepted sources are in attester-table.md. The admissibility rules are the ones in "What counts as a verification at all" above — the applicant may not carry the reply, and a source not on the table is raised.
office/procedure-extract.txt:107:Check 4 — Professional peer references
office/procedure-extract.txt:109:"IHS policy requires the collection of at least two peer references at the initial appointment. The"
office/procedure-extract.txt:110:"All peer references are from a professional authority who has worked directly with the applicant within the past two years and can authoritatively speak to the applicant's character, clinical experience, and competency."
office/procedure-extract.txt:115:* Worked together within two years is measured against the date the referee signs, because that is the day the referee attests to it. A referee whose last date working directly with the applicant is earlier than two years before their own signature date does not qualify. A blank last date means they still work together and the condition holds.
office/procedure-extract.txt:119:"Peer references are considered current if the reference's signature is within two years of the file presentation to the GB."
office/procedure-extract.txt:120:The signature date, not the date we received it. A reference can go stale while the file waits.
office/procedure-extract.txt:121:Larkhollow rule — when currency is measured. A reference is current when the presentation date is on or before the second anniversary of the signature date. For a file the Governing Body has decided, the presentation date is the decision date. For a file not yet decided, we measure currency against today, so that a reference about to go stale is visible before the committee meets rather than afterwards.
office/procedure-extract.txt:122:Larkhollow rule — the reference window. The manual states how many times to ask and does not state how long to wait. Ours: 21 calendar days per request, up to three requests. Request one goes out, request two 21 days later, request three 21 days after that. From day 64 after the first request the reference is overdue: we tell the applicant and ask for an additional referee. The original request stays open and stays outstanding; it is never closed as satisfied and never counted.
office/procedure-extract.txt:123:Larkhollow rule — the floor is two. Two qualifying, current references, both eligible on all three disqualifiers, both signed inside two years of the presentation date. An ineligible referee does not count towards the two even though the reply is in the file.
office/procedure-extract.txt:124:Larkhollow rule — an open request does not hold a met element. Once two qualifying, current references are on file, the peer-reference element is resolved. A request that is still open is carried on the action list until the file is presented and is then closed as no longer needed; it is never counted, and it does not hold the element or the file.
office/procedure-extract.txt:133:and Section 9 says what criteria must address:
office/procedure-extract.txt:134:"At a minimum, privilege criteria should address the required education level, formal training requirements, and current experience."
office/procedure-extract.txt:135:Larkhollow rule — the criteria are published and versioned. privilege-criteria.md maps each privilege group to the certifying boards that support it and to a minimum training requirement, under a version string. Every decision record cites the criteria version it was decided under. The office applies the map; the office does not write it and does not extend it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:142:Check 6 — The committee decision
office/procedure-extract.txt:147:"In addition, if any documents or verifications supporting the application illustrate that the applicant should have answered yes to a professional practice question but did not, the applicant is contacted to confirm the response."
office/procedure-extract.txt:175:and Section 8, on how long a verification stays good:
office/procedure-extract.txt:176:"Most of these verifications are required by accrediting organizations to be verified AT the time of appointment, the time between when the application is received and when it's reviewed."
office/procedure-extract.txt:177:The manual gave a fixed number once and removed it: its own change log for Version 5.0 records "Section 8: Removed 120-day expiration of primary source verifications."
office/procedure-extract.txt:178:Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. The anchor is the date revision 1 arrived, not the date of the current revision, so a later revision does not by itself void every verification already completed — what a revision invalidates is decided entry by entry, by reading what the revision actually changed. Peer references carry the additional two-year signature rule in check 4, which is stricter and wins where the two disagree.
office/procedure-extract.txt:179:Larkhollow rule — the board lookup and the window. A board lookup is the office's own check of the state board's public record on a day of the office's choosing, not a reply from a source, so the usability window is not applied to it: a lookup run on the decision day is usable for that decision. The date a packet became presentable is the date the last verification reply it needed was received; the lookup does not set it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:180:Larkhollow rule — what makes a packet presentable. Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is computed from the element statuses, not from anybody's recollection that the file looked finished.
office/procedure-extract.txt:181:For readiness, resolved means the element has nothing left to verify. An element carrying a finding is resolved in that sense once its evidence is with the Clinical Director — a licensure finding once the Clinical Director's disposition is on file, a certification finding on part of the request at once — and the packet is presented with the finding on it. An eligibility question, a gap awaiting the Clinical Director's disposition, an open discrepancy, an item returned to the applicant and a high-risk finding without its disposition are not resolved: while any of them stands, the packet is not presentable.
office/procedure-extract.txt:183:Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. A refused decision record does not undo it, and a withdrawn or discontinued file keeps the readiness its revision had: the office records what was ready, whatever the file did next. Only an element re-opening or a new revision changes it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:194:Larkhollow rule — what makes a decision admissible. All five, checked against the roster and the packet and never against the record's own claim:
office/procedure-extract.txt:196:2. the signatory held the named role on the decision date, per authority-roster.md;
office/procedure-extract.txt:197:3. the decision names the same applicant and the same application revision as the presentable packet;
office/procedure-extract.txt:198:4. a presentable packet existed for that revision before the decision date;
office/procedure-extract.txt:200:A decision that fails any of these is not a decision. It is recorded as received, raised to the Medical Services Professional, and nothing activates on it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:201:Larkhollow rule — a decision against a superseded revision. It does not authorize the current revision. It stays in the file as history against the revision it named, and it is never deleted.
office/procedure-extract.txt:202:Larkhollow rule — two decisions for one revision. A second decision for the same application revision is admissible only when it names the earlier decision it supersedes. Without that reference it is a duplicate, it is inadmissible, and it is raised to the Medical Services Professional. The first decision continues to stand.
office/procedure-extract.txt:203:Larkhollow rule — which outcomes carry a reason, and what counts as a second decision. recommended is the positive outcome of a body that cannot approve (the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff); like a plain approval it carries no reason, while not recommended carries one, as do approval-with-conditions, deferral and denial. The two-decisions rule above applies to a second decision of the same body for the same revision: a recommendation followed by the Governing Body's decision on the same revision is the normal sequence, not a duplicate, and a second recommendation is never a duplicate — so in practice it is a second Governing Body decision for the same revision that must name the earlier one it supersedes.
office/procedure-extract.txt:212:Larkhollow rule — activation. On an admitted Governing Body approval, the office records the appointment and activates exactly the privilege groups named in the decision — never more, and never a group that was requested but not granted. Privileges become active on the effective date the decision records, or on the decision date when the decision records no separate effective date. Nothing is active before that day. The cycle end is computed as in check 1.
office/procedure-extract.txt:228:	the licensure check re-runs on the new dates; a re-verification is placed in the file
office/procedure-extract.txt:229:	A decision that is not admissible, or that names a superseded revision

office/export-notes.txt:1:How this office exports its credentialing records
office/export-notes.txt:2:Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office A note from the Medical Services Professional to whoever automates the initial-appointment file. Written 2026-03-16, alongside the first export.
office/export-notes.txt:3:I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
office/export-notes.txt:4:The export date is the clock
office/export-notes.txt:5:Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
office/export-notes.txt:6:The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
office/export-notes.txt:7:The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
office/export-notes.txt:9:I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
office/export-notes.txt:12:Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
office/export-notes.txt:31:	verification-replies.csv
office/export-notes.txt:33:	verification-attempts.csv
office/export-notes.txt:37:	peer-reference-replies.csv
office/export-notes.txt:38:	one completed reference form that came back
office/export-notes.txt:40:	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
office/export-notes.txt:49:	decisions/
office/export-notes.txt:52:A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
office/export-notes.txt:53:Dates, blanks and columns
office/export-notes.txt:55:* An empty cell means I hold no value for that field. It does not mean zero, it does not mean "no", and it does not mean the answer is unknown-but-probably-fine. Two blanks carry a specific meaning and you should learn them:
office/export-notes.txt:56:   * a blank to_date in declared-history.csv means the entry is current, running to the export date — not that the end date is missing;
office/export-notes.txt:57:   * a blank expiry_date in certification-replies.csv means the certificate does not expire — some older certificates are time-unlimited.
office/export-notes.txt:62:2. The Washington board export carries no practitioner identifier. It never has. I join it to an application on lastname, firstname, middlename and birthyear. I have checked that no two rows in any one export share those four values, so the join gives you at most one row. An applicant with no row in that file holds no Washington credential. The absence is the answer, not a data problem.
office/export-notes.txt:63:3. A referee with no row in peer-reference-replies.csv has not replied. Silence produces no record. You can see it only by looking at the requests in verification-attempts.csv and finding no reply against them.
office/export-notes.txt:64:The Washington export's own columns
office/export-notes.txt:69:The first export carries the board's whole file for our county — 435 rows — so you can see what an ordinary population looks like. The second and third carry only a re-lookup of the practitioners whose files are open, because that is all I re-run.
office/export-notes.txt:72:In the board's population, action against a credential is rare. In the 435-row export you have: 431 rows say No, 3 say Yes, and 1 says Pending. That is 0.69% Yes and 0.23% Pending, and it is the shape of the real thing — the overwhelming majority of licensed practitioners have a clean board record, and any tool that expects otherwise will be wrong almost every time it fires.
office/export-notes.txt:73:The applicants in these batches are a different matter, and deliberately so. This is a teaching set. I have put every situation the procedure has a rule for into these three exports on purpose, so the run has something to exercise: a restricted licence, an unexplained gap, a school that closed, a referee who never answers, a certificate that lapsed, a decision against the wrong revision. A real nine weeks of intake would be far quieter than this. Do not read the applicant set as a base rate. Read it as a checklist that happens to be shaped like a caseload.
office/export-notes.txt:75:What I do not export
office/export-notes.txt:76:My own queue, my own statuses and my own conclusions. This export is the evidence, not my reading of it. What is complete, what is outstanding, what is presentable and what is owed to whom is the work — it is not in the folder, and it should not be.
office/export-notes.txt:77:Referee addresses. The export carries no address column for peer referees. The working-address half of completeness condition 7 is checked by my office outside the export, so a run assesses condition 7 on the named referees alone and records the address check as not assessable from the export — neither met nor failed.

office/procedure-extract.txt:5:Larkhollow is a community hospital. It is not a federal facility. We adopted the verification standard work published by the Indian Health Service in its Medical Staff Credentialing and Privileging Standard Operating Procedure Manual, Version 8.0, September 2025, as our own written procedure, because it is a complete, current and publicly stated account of how the work is done.
office/procedure-extract.txt:10:The office also runs identity verification, controlled-substance registrations, the National Practitioner Data Bank query, sanctions and exclusion lookups, life support certificates, continuing education, immunization records, liability coverage and malpractice history. Those are handled outside this procedure and are not part of the work described here.
office/procedure-extract.txt:17:"a signed IHS Conditions of Application & Release is received (required to be able to conduct any verifications);"
office/procedure-extract.txt:19:Larkhollow rule. Our equivalent of that release is the Larkhollow Authorization and Release, printed inside the application. It is our own form; the manual's is a federal instrument and we do not use it. The rule it carries is the manual's and we keep it: until a signed release is on file we send no verification request of any kind. A file with no signed release cannot advance, no matter how much else is present.
office/procedure-extract.txt:27:7. at least two peer referees are named, with a working address for each;
office/procedure-extract.txt:28:8. every declared affiliation and employer carries a verification contact;
office/procedure-extract.txt:36:Before and during verification we read the curriculum vitae against the application, and then both against whatever the sources return. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
office/procedure-extract.txt:37:"The MSP will compare the CV/resume with the application and completed verifications and correct or resolve any discrepancies."
office/procedure-extract.txt:38:"There must be a follow-up of any verification discrepancies found during the application and"
office/procedure-extract.txt:45:Larkhollow rule — a revision is reconciled, not assumed. When a revision arrives, the reconciliation above runs again on what the revision says, against the curriculum vitae and against every verification already completed on the entries it touches. Dates are not the only thing a revision can move: the organization, the role, the supervisor and the verification contact all belong to the entry, and a change to any of them is a change to the entry. Section 11 says what re-opens when it does. The monitoring duty in section 11 runs alongside it and does not pause while a file waits.
office/procedure-extract.txt:47:Six elements are verified in this procedure: licensure, experience, time gaps, professional education and post-graduate training, board certification, and professional peer references. The manual numbers seventeen essential credentialing elements in Section 6, Subsection 4. Of the other eleven, nine are handled by the office outside this procedure, as stated above; current competency is the clinical leadership's, not the office's; and the manual's conditions-and-release form is replaced by our own Authorization and Release, which is part of intake in this procedure.
office/procedure-extract.txt:48:What counts as a verification at all
office/procedure-extract.txt:49:The manual, Section 1, defines primary source verification as
office/procedure-extract.txt:52:"Primary source verifications received directly from the applicant cannot be used."
office/procedure-extract.txt:53:"Copies of a diploma, license, registration, etc., in place of verifications are unacceptable."
office/procedure-extract.txt:54:A reply that reached us through the applicant is not a verification, however genuine the document looks, however clear the letterhead, however real the registrar's signature. It goes in the file as received and the request stays open.
office/procedure-extract.txt:56:"etc., as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for education and training verifications"
office/procedure-extract.txt:58:"or other nationally recognized certifying body, as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for board certification verifications"
office/procedure-extract.txt:61:"If completing primary or DES verifications is impossible, such as when an educational institution or residency program has closed, secondary source verifications may be used."
office/procedure-extract.txt:62:"When a primary or designated equivalent source cannot be obtained, the applicant's recent affiliations should be contacted to discover how they obtained the verification."
office/procedure-extract.txt:67:"Each attempt, including whom it was attempted to verify with, the date of request, verification methods, and any additional comments, is documented in the Notes section of the entry."
office/procedure-extract.txt:70:"If the affiliation is unwilling to complete the verification or is non-responsive after 3 attempts, this should be noted as a red flag."
office/procedure-extract.txt:85:"For IHS, initial appointments are one year long, and reappointments are two years long, regardless of accrediting body medical staff standards or medical staff bylaws."
office/procedure-extract.txt:86:The cycle starts on the date the appointment takes effect and ends one year later minus one day, so a cycle starting 2026-05-01 ends 2027-04-30. The Washington licence must be valid on the decision date. If it expires inside the cycle, that is not a denial and it is not a pass: it is recorded as a monitored condition with a re-verification due date set before the expiry date, and it does not block activation. If the re-verification fails, the file re-opens. The due date recorded on the condition is the licence's expiry date itself; "before" says when the re-verification must be complete, not what the recorded date is.
office/procedure-extract.txt:96:Larkhollow rule — how the gap list is computed. The clock starts on the day after the applicant finished professional school. Every declared entry of any type covers every day from its start date to its end date inclusive; an entry with no end date runs to the export date. Overlapping entries, part-time appointments and training years are covering entries: an overlap covers, it does not create a gap. A gap is a run of 30 or more consecutive days that no entry covers. The list is recomputed from scratch whenever a revision or a verification changes a date; it is not patched.
office/procedure-extract.txt:104:So: the qualifying degree, and every post-graduate training entry. The accepted sources are in attester-table.md. The admissibility rules are the ones in "What counts as a verification at all" above — the applicant may not carry the reply, and a source not on the table is raised.
office/procedure-extract.txt:107:Check 4 — Professional peer references
office/procedure-extract.txt:109:"IHS policy requires the collection of at least two peer references at the initial appointment. The"
office/procedure-extract.txt:110:"All peer references are from a professional authority who has worked directly with the applicant within the past two years and can authoritatively speak to the applicant's character, clinical experience, and competency."
office/procedure-extract.txt:115:* Worked together within two years is measured against the date the referee signs, because that is the day the referee attests to it. A referee whose last date working directly with the applicant is earlier than two years before their own signature date does not qualify. A blank last date means they still work together and the condition holds.
office/procedure-extract.txt:119:"Peer references are considered current if the reference's signature is within two years of the file presentation to the GB."
office/procedure-extract.txt:120:The signature date, not the date we received it. A reference can go stale while the file waits.
office/procedure-extract.txt:121:Larkhollow rule — when currency is measured. A reference is current when the presentation date is on or before the second anniversary of the signature date. For a file the Governing Body has decided, the presentation date is the decision date. For a file not yet decided, we measure currency against today, so that a reference about to go stale is visible before the committee meets rather than afterwards.
office/procedure-extract.txt:122:Larkhollow rule — the reference window. The manual states how many times to ask and does not state how long to wait. Ours: 21 calendar days per request, up to three requests. Request one goes out, request two 21 days later, request three 21 days after that. From day 64 after the first request the reference is overdue: we tell the applicant and ask for an additional referee. The original request stays open and stays outstanding; it is never closed as satisfied and never counted.
office/procedure-extract.txt:123:Larkhollow rule — the floor is two. Two qualifying, current references, both eligible on all three disqualifiers, both signed inside two years of the presentation date. An ineligible referee does not count towards the two even though the reply is in the file.
office/procedure-extract.txt:124:Larkhollow rule — an open request does not hold a met element. Once two qualifying, current references are on file, the peer-reference element is resolved. A request that is still open is carried on the action list until the file is presented and is then closed as no longer needed; it is never counted, and it does not hold the element or the file.
office/procedure-extract.txt:133:and Section 9 says what criteria must address:
office/procedure-extract.txt:134:"At a minimum, privilege criteria should address the required education level, formal training requirements, and current experience."
office/procedure-extract.txt:135:Larkhollow rule — the criteria are published and versioned. privilege-criteria.md maps each privilege group to the certifying boards that support it and to a minimum training requirement, under a version string. Every decision record cites the criteria version it was decided under. The office applies the map; the office does not write it and does not extend it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:142:Check 6 — The committee decision
office/procedure-extract.txt:147:"In addition, if any documents or verifications supporting the application illustrate that the applicant should have answered yes to a professional practice question but did not, the applicant is contacted to confirm the response."
office/procedure-extract.txt:175:and Section 8, on how long a verification stays good:
office/procedure-extract.txt:176:"Most of these verifications are required by accrediting organizations to be verified AT the time of appointment, the time between when the application is received and when it's reviewed."
office/procedure-extract.txt:177:The manual gave a fixed number once and removed it: its own change log for Version 5.0 records "Section 8: Removed 120-day expiration of primary source verifications."
office/procedure-extract.txt:178:Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. The anchor is the date revision 1 arrived, not the date of the current revision, so a later revision does not by itself void every verification already completed — what a revision invalidates is decided entry by entry, by reading what the revision actually changed. Peer references carry the additional two-year signature rule in check 4, which is stricter and wins where the two disagree.
office/procedure-extract.txt:179:Larkhollow rule — the board lookup and the window. A board lookup is the office's own check of the state board's public record on a day of the office's choosing, not a reply from a source, so the usability window is not applied to it: a lookup run on the decision day is usable for that decision. The date a packet became presentable is the date the last verification reply it needed was received; the lookup does not set it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:180:Larkhollow rule — what makes a packet presentable. Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is computed from the element statuses, not from anybody's recollection that the file looked finished.
office/procedure-extract.txt:181:For readiness, resolved means the element has nothing left to verify. An element carrying a finding is resolved in that sense once its evidence is with the Clinical Director — a licensure finding once the Clinical Director's disposition is on file, a certification finding on part of the request at once — and the packet is presented with the finding on it. An eligibility question, a gap awaiting the Clinical Director's disposition, an open discrepancy, an item returned to the applicant and a high-risk finding without its disposition are not resolved: while any of them stands, the packet is not presentable.
office/procedure-extract.txt:183:Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. A refused decision record does not undo it, and a withdrawn or discontinued file keeps the readiness its revision had: the office records what was ready, whatever the file did next. Only an element re-opening or a new revision changes it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:194:Larkhollow rule — what makes a decision admissible. All five, checked against the roster and the packet and never against the record's own claim:
office/procedure-extract.txt:196:2. the signatory held the named role on the decision date, per authority-roster.md;
office/procedure-extract.txt:197:3. the decision names the same applicant and the same application revision as the presentable packet;
office/procedure-extract.txt:198:4. a presentable packet existed for that revision before the decision date;
office/procedure-extract.txt:200:A decision that fails any of these is not a decision. It is recorded as received, raised to the Medical Services Professional, and nothing activates on it.
office/procedure-extract.txt:201:Larkhollow rule — a decision against a superseded revision. It does not authorize the current revision. It stays in the file as history against the revision it named, and it is never deleted.
office/procedure-extract.txt:202:Larkhollow rule — two decisions for one revision. A second decision for the same application revision is admissible only when it names the earlier decision it supersedes. Without that reference it is a duplicate, it is inadmissible, and it is raised to the Medical Services Professional. The first decision continues to stand.
office/procedure-extract.txt:203:Larkhollow rule — which outcomes carry a reason, and what counts as a second decision. recommended is the positive outcome of a body that cannot approve (the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff); like a plain approval it carries no reason, while not recommended carries one, as do approval-with-conditions, deferral and denial. The two-decisions rule above applies to a second decision of the same body for the same revision: a recommendation followed by the Governing Body's decision on the same revision is the normal sequence, not a duplicate, and a second recommendation is never a duplicate — so in practice it is a second Governing Body decision for the same revision that must name the earlier one it supersedes.
office/procedure-extract.txt:212:Larkhollow rule — activation. On an admitted Governing Body approval, the office records the appointment and activates exactly the privilege groups named in the decision — never more, and never a group that was requested but not granted. Privileges become active on the effective date the decision records, or on the decision date when the decision records no separate effective date. Nothing is active before that day. The cycle end is computed as in check 1.

office/export-notes.txt:1:How this office exports its credentialing records
office/export-notes.txt:2:Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office A note from the Medical Services Professional to whoever automates the initial-appointment file. Written 2026-03-16, alongside the first export.
office/export-notes.txt:3:I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
office/export-notes.txt:4:The export date is the clock
office/export-notes.txt:5:Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
office/export-notes.txt:6:The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
office/export-notes.txt:7:The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
office/export-notes.txt:9:I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
office/export-notes.txt:12:Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
office/export-notes.txt:31:	verification-replies.csv
office/export-notes.txt:33:	verification-attempts.csv
office/export-notes.txt:37:	peer-reference-replies.csv
office/export-notes.txt:38:	one completed reference form that came back
office/export-notes.txt:40:	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
office/export-notes.txt:49:	decisions/
office/export-notes.txt:52:A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
office/export-notes.txt:53:Dates, blanks and columns
office/export-notes.txt:55:* An empty cell means I hold no value for that field. It does not mean zero, it does not mean "no", and it does not mean the answer is unknown-but-probably-fine. Two blanks carry a specific meaning and you should learn them:
office/export-notes.txt:56:   * a blank to_date in declared-history.csv means the entry is current, running to the export date — not that the end date is missing;
office/export-notes.txt:57:   * a blank expiry_date in certification-replies.csv means the certificate does not expire — some older certificates are time-unlimited.
office/export-notes.txt:62:2. The Washington board export carries no practitioner identifier. It never has. I join it to an application on lastname, firstname, middlename and birthyear. I have checked that no two rows in any one export share those four values, so the join gives you at most one row. An applicant with no row in that file holds no Washington credential. The absence is the answer, not a data problem.
office/export-notes.txt:63:3. A referee with no row in peer-reference-replies.csv has not replied. Silence produces no record. You can see it only by looking at the requests in verification-attempts.csv and finding no reply against them.
office/export-notes.txt:64:The Washington export's own columns
office/export-notes.txt:69:The first export carries the board's whole file for our county — 435 rows — so you can see what an ordinary population looks like. The second and third carry only a re-lookup of the practitioners whose files are open, because that is all I re-run.
office/export-notes.txt:72:In the board's population, action against a credential is rare. In the 435-row export you have: 431 rows say No, 3 say Yes, and 1 says Pending. That is 0.69% Yes and 0.23% Pending, and it is the shape of the real thing — the overwhelming majority of licensed practitioners have a clean board record, and any tool that expects otherwise will be wrong almost every time it fires.
office/export-notes.txt:73:The applicants in these batches are a different matter, and deliberately so. This is a teaching set. I have put every situation the procedure has a rule for into these three exports on purpose, so the run has something to exercise: a restricted licence, an unexplained gap, a school that closed, a referee who never answers, a certificate that lapsed, a decision against the wrong revision. A real nine weeks of intake would be far quieter than this. Do not read the applicant set as a base rate. Read it as a checklist that happens to be shaped like a caseload.
office/export-notes.txt:75:What I do not export
office/export-notes.txt:76:My own queue, my own statuses and my own conclusions. This export is the evidence, not my reading of it. What is complete, what is outstanding, what is presentable and what is owed to whom is the work — it is not in the folder, and it should not be.
office/export-notes.txt:77:Referee addresses. The export carries no address column for peer referees. The working-address half of completeness condition 7 is checked by my office outside the export, so a run assesses condition 7 on the named referees alone and records the address check as not assessable from the export — neither met nor failed.
